Elias sat in the back row of the symphony hall, his violin case open on his lap. The orchestra was playing Tchaikovsky, a piece he had performed a hundred times, but the sound that reached his ears was not the music on the page. It was a jagged, dissonant shriek, like metal tearing through glass.
He closed his eyes, trying to isolate the source. The conductor’s baton moved in precise, mathematical arcs, but the melody Elias heard was chaotic, spiraling inward like a drain. He could see the cellist’s bow trembling, not from effort, but from a subtle, involuntary twitch. The flutist’s fingers were moving a fraction of a second too late.
To the audience, the music was swelling into a triumphant crescendo. To Elias, it was a scream.
He had heard this before. Not in concerts, but in the quiet moments of his own life. A phone ringing in an empty room sounded like a child crying. The hum of the refrigerator was a low, mournful cello note. The world was not silent to him; it was overloaded. Every vibration carried a hidden, secondary melody that only he could perceive.
He picked up his bow, not to play, but to test the air. He drew it across the strings, a single, sustained note. To the few people nearby, it was a beautiful, pure tone. To Elias, it was a door opening.
